t: Number of Visible People in a Queue -- Monotonic Stack Visibility
o: Person i sees person j to their right exactly when everyone standing between them is shorter than both heights. Walking through [10,6,8,5,11,9]: person 0 sees persons 1, 2 and 4 (person 3, height 5, is hidden because the people in between are taller than 5), person 1 sees only person 2, person 2 sees persons 3 and 4, person 3 sees person 4, person 4 sees person 5, and the last person sees nobody -- giving [3,1,2,1,1,0]. Heights are distinct and n reaches 10^5, so testing all pairs (roughly n^2/2 comparisons) is far too slow and motivates a single right-to-left pass with a monotonic stack.
k: When scanning right to left, every stack entry popped by height h is shorter than h with nothing taller in between, so each pop is exactly one person that the current person can see.
After popping, the surviving stack top is the nearest person at least as tall -- also visible, supplying the +1.
The stack always holds a strictly decreasing sequence of heights, and every index is pushed and popped at most once, giving linear time.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force Scan With Running Maximum
a.i: From each person i, walk right keeping the tallest height seen so far. Person j is visible exactly when the running maximum (everyone between) is below heights[j]; once that running maximum reaches heights[i], nobody further right can ever be visible, so the scan stops early.
s: For each i, initialize tallest = 0 and scan j from i + 1 onward.
Break the scan once tallest >= heights[i] -- the view is permanently blocked.
Otherwise count j when heights[j] > tallest and update tallest to heights[j].
a.t: O(n^2) worst case -- each starting index may scan across a long decreasing run
a.sp: O(1) -- only the answer array plus one scalar

a.i: Process people from right to left keeping a stack of heights that might still be seen by people further left, strictly decreasing bottom to top. Popping every height below heights[i] counts exactly the people i can see -- each was waiting behind someone no taller than themselves -- and the remaining top, if any, is the nearest taller person, who is also visible.
s: Initialize an empty stack and an all-zero answer array.
For i from n - 1 down to 0: pop and count every stack height below heights[i].
If the stack still has someone, add 1 for that nearest taller person.
Push heights[i] and continue; the last person naturally ends with 0.
a.t: O(n) -- each height is pushed once and popped at most once
a.sp: O(n) -- the stack can hold an entire strictly decreasing suffix

w: Jump straight to the monotonic stack once n rules out the quadratic scan; the equivalent left-to-right variant credits popped indices and the new stack top with a visible count. Pitfalls: forgetting the +1 for the surviving stack top is the classic bug; strict versus non-strict comparisons do not collide here because heights are distinct. Edge cases: n = 1 returns [0], and a strictly decreasing queue makes everyone see exactly one person. Likely follow-ups: visibility in both directions, or answering many queries fast -- solvable by binary searching the furthest visible person with a sparse-table range maximum.
